title: Lexicographically Smallest String After Adjacent Removals
summary: Given a string of lowercase letters, repeatedly remove any adjacent characters that are consecutive in the alphabet, then shift the remaining characters left.
statement: Given a string of lowercase letters, repeatedly remove any adjacent characters that are consecutive in the alphabet, then shift the remaining characters left. Return the lexicographically smallest string possible after optimally performing these operations, treating 'a' and 'z' as consecutive.
constraints: s contains up to 250 lowercase letters.
Remove any adjacent alphabet-consecutive pair in either order, with circular a-z adjacency.
Operations are optional; return the lexicographically smallest reachable string.
hints: Two characters can become adjacent exactly when the entire interval between them can be deleted.
First compute which intervals can vanish; then build the smallest suffix by either keeping its first character or pairing it across a vanishing interior.
Fill empty[left][right] by possible partners, then set best[left] to the minimum of s[left]+best[left+1] and best[partner+1].
Every valid result either keeps its first original character or removes it with one uniquely exposed partner; these cases exhaust the first operation affecting that character.
editorial: Every valid result either keeps its first original character or removes it with one uniquely exposed partner; these cases exhaust the first operation affecting that character.

tests.explanation: Removing bc leaves a, which is lexicographically smallest.
Although dc can be removed, keeping the original zdce is smaller than ze.
